nodes.title: Progressive Waves & Characteristics
points: A progressive wave continuously travels in a medium, transferring energy and momentum without the physical transfer of matter.
Displacement equation (wave traveling along +x): y = A sin(ωt − kx) = A sin 2π(t/T − x/λ).
Wavenumber / propagation constant: k = 2π/λ = ω/v (SI unit: rad/m).
Wave speed: v = nλ = λ/T = ω/k.
Phase difference and path difference link: Δϕ = (2π/λ) × Δx; Phase difference and time interval link: Δϕ = (2π/T) × Δt.
Particle velocity v_p = dy/dt = ω√(A² − y²); Maximum particle velocity v_p(max) = ωA.

nodes.title: Superposition Principle & Reflection of Waves
points: Principle of Superposition: When two or more waves arrive at a point simultaneously, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of individual displacements: y = y₁ + y₂.
Reflection from Denser (Rigid) Boundary: Reflected wave undergoes a phase reversal of π rad (180°). Crest reflects as trough, compression reflects as rarefaction.
Reflection from Rarer (Free) Boundary: Reflected wave undergoes NO phase change (Δϕ = 0). Crest reflects as crest, compression reflects as compression.
Amplitude of reflected wave: From rigid boundary, displacement is zero at the boundary (node forms); at free boundary, antinode forms.

nodes.title: Stationary Waves: Formation & Characteristics
points: Stationary (standing) waves form when two identical progressive waves traveling in opposite directions along the same line superpose.
Equation: y = y₁ + y₂ = (2A cos kx) sin ωt = R sin ωt, where amplitude R = 2A cos(2πx/λ).
Nodes: Points of zero displacement (R = 0), where cos kx = 0 ⟹ x = (2p + 1)λ/4. Strain is maximum at nodes.
Antinodes: Points of maximum displacement (R = ±2A), where cos kx = ±1 ⟹ x = pλ/2. Strain is minimum (zero) at antinodes.
Distance between two successive nodes or antinodes = λ/2; Distance between adjacent node and antinode = λ/4.
Stationary waves do NOT propagate energy; particles in the same loop vibrate in phase; particles in adjacent loops vibrate in opposite phase.

nodes.title: Vibrations of Stretched String & Sonometer
points: Speed of transverse wave on a string: v = √(T/m), where T is tension and m is linear density (mass per unit length m = M/L = πr²ρ).
Fundamental frequency (1st harmonic, 1 loop): n = v / (2L) = (1 / 2L) √(T / m).
p-th harmonic frequency (p loops): n_p = p × n = (p / 2L) √(T / m). ALL harmonics (odd and even) are present.
Laws of Vibrating Strings: (1) Law of length: n ∝ 1/L (T, m const); (2) Law of tension: n ∝ √T (L, m const); (3) Law of linear density: n ∝ 1/√m (L, T const).
Sonometer verifies these laws by resonating a wire of variable length with known tuning forks using a light paper rider.

nodes.title: Air Columns: Pipe Closed at One End
points: Boundary condition: Node at closed end, antinode at open end.
Fundamental mode (1st harmonic): L = λ/4 ⟹ λ = 4L ⟹ n = v / (4L).
First overtone (3rd harmonic): L = 3λ/4 ⟹ n₁ = 3v / (4L) = 3n.
Second overtone (5th harmonic): L = 5λ/4 ⟹ n₂ = 5v / (4L) = 5n.
Key Property: In a pipe closed at one end, ONLY ODD harmonics are present: n, 3n, 5n, 7n, ... (even harmonics are absent).
p-th overtone frequency: n_p = (2p + 1) n.

nodes.title: Air Columns: Pipe Open at Both Ends
points: Boundary condition: Antinodes at both open ends, node in between.
Fundamental mode (1st harmonic): L = λ/2 ⟹ λ = 2L ⟹ n' = v / (2L).
First overtone (2nd harmonic): L = λ ⟹ n₁' = 2v / (2L) = 2n'.
Second overtone (3rd harmonic): L = 3λ/2 ⟹ n₂' = 3v / (2L) = 3n'.
Key Property: In a pipe open at both ends, ALL harmonics (odd and even) are present: n', 2n', 3n', 4n', ...
Comparison: For same physical length L, open pipe frequency is DOUBLE the closed pipe frequency: n_open = 2 × n_closed.

nodes.title: End Correction & Musical Characteristics
points: End correction (e): The antinode at the open end is formed slightly outside the open end at distance e = 0.3 d, where d is the inner diameter.
Pipe closed at one end: Corrected length L' = L + e = L + 0.3 d ⟹ n = v / [4(L + 0.3 d)].
Pipe open at both ends: Corrected length L' = L + 2e = L + 0.6 d ⟹ n' = v / [2(L + 0.6 d)].
Resonance tube experiment: e = (v/4)(1/n₁ − 1/n₂) or e = (l₂ − 3l₁)/2, and speed of sound v = 2n(l₂ − l₁).
Characteristics of Musical Sound: Loudness (depends on intensity I ∝ A²), Pitch (depends on frequency n), Quality/Timbre (depends on the number and nature of overtones present).

nodes.title: Beats: Theory & Applications
points: Beats: Periodic variation in intensity of sound produced when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies superpose along the same line.
Waxing: Maximum intensity; Waning: Minimum intensity. One waxing and one waning constitute one beat.
Beat frequency: n_b = |n₁ − n₂| (number of beats heard per second).
Period of beats: T_b = 1 / n_b = 1 / |n₁ − n₂|.
For distinct beats to be heard by human ear, |n₁ − n₂| ≤ 10 Hz (due to persistence of hearing = 0.1 s).
Applications: Tuning musical instruments to standard pitch, detecting dangerous marsh gas (methane) in mines.

nodes.title: Must-Know Board Derivations & Distinctions
points: Board Favourite #1: Derive analytical expression for stationary waves on a stretched string and locate positions of nodes and antinodes.
Board Favourite #2: Show that only odd harmonics are present in a pipe closed at one end, whereas all harmonics are present in an open pipe.
Board Favourite #3: Derive expression for beat frequency n_b = n₁ − n₂ from the principle of superposition of waves.

Distinction #1: Progressive waves (transmit energy, all particles have same amplitude, phase changes continuously) vs Stationary waves (no energy transmission, amplitude varies from 0 to 2A, particles in same loop have same phase).
Distinction #2: Harmonics (integral multiples of fundamental frequency) vs Overtones (frequencies higher than fundamental actually emitted by instrument).

nodes.title: MHT-CET Tuning Fork Traps & Speed Hacks
points: Tuning Fork Loading Rule: When a tuning fork is loaded with wax, its frequency DECREASES (n falls).
Tuning Fork Filing Rule: When the prongs of a tuning fork are filed, its mass decreases and its frequency INCREASES (n rises).
Beat Frequency Deduction Shortcut: If fork A (known n_A) produces 4 beats/s with B, then n_B = n_A ± 4. If loading A decreases beat frequency, then n_A > n_B.
Effect of Temperature on Pipe Frequency: v ∝ √T ⟹ frequency n ∝ √T (temperature in Kelvin). Pipe frequency increases on hot days.
String Submerged in Water: Tension T_eff = T(1 − σ/ρ) ⟹ frequency n' = n √(1 − σ/ρ), where σ is liquid density and ρ is wire density.
Open vs Closed Comparison: If open pipe is dipped half in water, it becomes a closed pipe of same length L/2, so fundamental frequency remains the same!
